d.title: Five stages, cheapest at the top
d.caption: **A plan that describes only the fourth row pays the maximum cost every time.** Prevention is design work, so it loses to features unless somebody argues for it; detection is cheap and bounds everything below it, because nothing is contained or recovered faster than it is noticed. **Verification is the other cheap one, and omitting it is how a silent regression ships** — a restore that returns 200 has been checked for liveness, which was never the property at risk.

items.label: Prevent
items.sub: immutable artifacts, pinned deps, idempotency keys, retention on the source

items.label: Detect
items.sub: freshness, canary queries, eval scores in monitoring, drift alarms

items.label: Contain
items.sub: degraded mode, blue-green, circuit breakers, load shedding

items.label: Recover
items.sub: snapshots, point-in-time, rebuild pipelines, a second provider

items.label: Verify
items.sub: evals against a dated baseline, reconciliation, golden outputs

d.title: One pair of numbers, applied to six assets that disagree
d.caption: **A single system-wide RTO is an average of things with nothing in common** — and the moment it is written down, the plan is wrong for every asset at once. Here a stated four-hour RTO is comfortable for four rows and arithmetically impossible for one: **the index cannot be rebuilt in four hours, so the plan commits to something nobody has checked.** Per-asset numbers make that visible on the page rather than during the incident.

d.title: What is source, what is derived, and the one that only looks derived
d.caption: **Read it as two piles.** Everything on the right can be recomputed, so its recovery is a question of time and money. Everything on the left cannot, so it needs real backups and a named owner. **The trap is in the middle: a vector index is derived from the documents, which makes it recoverable only while the documents exist somewhere else** — and in a RAG system that somewhere is frequently another team's system with its own retention policy.

d.title: Six hours against eleven minutes, for the same asset
d.caption: **The plan called the index “derived, so we can rebuild it”, and that sentence is a six-hour commitment.** Measuring it takes one batch of embeddings and some arithmetic, and it reverses the decision: snapshot the derived asset, because otherwise rebuild time *is* your recovery time. **Keep the rebuild path working anyway** — it is the only answer to a corrupt snapshot, to a bad write the snapshot also contains, and to documents that have changed since it was taken.

d.title: Degrade first, then fail over - and never ship a fallback that takes no traffic
d.caption: **There is no standby to promote, so the first question is not “which second provider” but “what does this system do with no model at all”.** For RAG the answer is unusually good: return the retrieved passages without a generated summary, and say so. **A second provider is worth having and is not a hot standby:** the prompts were tuned against the primary, so the secondary returns different answers and may reject your output schema outright. One per cent of traffic, continuously, is what turns it from a plan into something already working.

nodes.sub: an outage is a delay, not an incident

d.title: The checkpointer restores the graph; it does not un-send the email
d.caption: **The run died between the side effect and the checkpoint, which is the one ordering that makes resumption dangerous.** The graph is restored correctly to a node that has already acted, so the resume charges the card a second time — no error, and the state machine behaving exactly as designed. **The fix is a key derived from the run id, not from the attempt:** a fresh key per retry is indistinguishable from a new request and defeats the whole mechanism. Lesson 16.4 is this row by row.

d.title: Six stages, and only one of them fails loudly
d.caption: **This is the column that makes ML recovery a different discipline rather than an application of the usual one.** Four of the six characteristic failures complete successfully, return a number, and move on — so the question “what broke” cannot be answered by looking at errors, and the mitigation cannot be chosen until the stage is located. **The registry is the only stage that fails loudly, and only at the moment you try to use it.**

d.title: Why freshness is the assertion that catches the most incidents
d.caption: **A pipeline that reprocesses yesterday's file succeeds every time.** Every row is valid, the schema passes, the volume is identical, and the model trains on data that is one day stale — so no row-level validation can possibly notice. One comparison of the maximum timestamp against today catches it, and it is the cheapest assertion in the pipeline. **The volume check is the companion:** compare against the recent average, not against zero, because a truncated export is a plausible row count and so is a doubled one.

nodes.sub: against zero, which is the usual check

Freshness: max timestamp is today

d.title: What has to be recorded for a training run to be rebuildable
d.caption: **Two of these fields are the ones that turn provenance from a formality into a guarantee.** A commit sha recorded from a working tree with uncommitted changes describes code that exists nowhere, so the artifact claims a reproducibility it does not have — which is why `git_dirty` belongs beside it. **And the label cutoff is the ML-specific one:** a 90-day outcome cannot be observed for a row extracted 30 days ago, so the most recent rows carry systematically wrong labels, and they are the rows most like production.

state: the sha describes code that does not exist

d.title: Four restore checks, and only the last one catches a wrong version
d.caption: **Every row above the last passes on an older artifact of the same model.** It loads, it serves, the latency is normal and the health check is green — because none of those checks is about identity. **Golden predictions are a few dozen input rows and their expected outputs, committed to git**, and they fail immediately on a wrong version. It is the cheapest verification in ML recovery and almost nobody has it; reporting the version and schema hash from the health endpoint is the other half, because it makes the identity visible from outside.

d.title: Seven stages, each computed from the one before it
d.caption: **The dependency runs left to right, which is what makes stage 1 the only true single point of failure** — everything after it is recomputable, and recomputable only while the documents exist somewhere you control. So the first recovery question for a RAG system is not “what is the backup” but **“where is the copy of the corpus that is not in the index”**, and the answer frequently names a system owned by another team. The last two stages are stateless: nothing to lose, and all of the detection burden.

d.title: Two indexes, both valid, not interchangeable
d.caption: **Nothing inside an index records the configuration that produced it**, so a restored index built with 400-token chunks instead of 800 answers every query, returns plausible passages, and retrieves measurably worse — which is exactly the incident at the end of lesson 16.1. The fingerprint is a hash of the parser version, chunk size, overlap, splitter and embedding model, written into the index metadata and the snapshot's name. **Then a restore can assert that what came back matches the code that is running**, which is the difference between a verifiable restore and a hopeful one.

d.title: A retired embedding model freezes an index rather than breaking it
d.caption: **The stored vectors are perfectly fine and stop meaning the same thing.** Queries go through the replacement model into a different space, cosine similarity still returns a number, and the number is meaningless — so there is no error, normal latency, plausible passages, and recall off a cliff. A corrupted index would at least have failed loudly. **Two cheap things catch or prevent it:** a dozen canary query-document pairs on a schedule, and the model identity recorded in the index with a refusal to query on a mismatch.

nodes.label: Or refuse to query on a mismatch

d.title: Which path recovers which failure
d.caption: **Neither path covers everything, which is the argument for keeping both rather than choosing one.** The snapshot is the fast path and the rebuild is the only answer to a corrupt snapshot or a configuration change. **Rows four and five are where the snapshot wins and the rebuild cannot help at all** — both are cases where the corpus or the model moved rather than the index breaking, and a rebuild faithfully reproduces the problem.

d.title: Five stages replay freely; the sixth changes the world
d.caption: **One row says no, and it makes agentic recovery a different problem from everything else in this module.** Planning, model calls and read-only tools cost tokens and change nothing, so replaying them is a billing question. A side-effecting tool call has already happened in a system you do not control. **And the state write is why it matters: the checkpoint is persisted after the action**, so a crash in between leaves a world that has changed and a state that does not know it.

d.title: Three mechanisms, and the one-character difference that breaks the first
d.caption: **Row two is the most common way idempotency is implemented wrongly, and it passes review because the argument is present and correctly named.** A key generated per attempt is indistinguishable from a genuinely new request, so the provider deduplicates nothing — and the defect only appears when a process dies, which is not a thing tests do. **Row four is the cleanest mechanism where it is available:** a unique reference in the target system means the second attempt fails on a constraint you catch and treat as success, with no extra state of your own.

d.title: What the checkpointer holds decides its RPO
d.caption: **The worst case sets the number, and it is row four.** A run paused awaiting approval may have been created on Monday and approved on Thursday; losing it loses a request the user believes they made, and there is no source to re-derive it from. **That makes the database a system of record rather than a cache**, however temporary its contents look — so point-in-time recovery in minutes, not a nightly dump. And the ledger belongs in the same instance, or a restore can put the two at different timestamps and reintroduce the duplicate-action bug.

state: NOTHING - the state is the request

d.title: Six kinds of in-flight work, decided before the incident
d.caption: **Row four is the one that has to be written down in advance**, because it is a per-workflow fact nobody can recall at three in the morning: which workflows contain a side effect with no idempotency mechanism. A ten-line list turns “can we replay the queue?” from an unanswerable question into a lookup. **And the sweep should report counts** — resumed, dropped, dead-lettered — because a recovery that cannot say how many runs need human attention has stopped rather than finished.

state: a human decides, with the ledger

d.title: Four limits, and the one that catches the worst case soonest
d.caption: **An agent can take twenty-four steps, stay under budget, never hand off, and make no progress at all** — retrying the same failing tool call with the same arguments. The step and budget caps are both eventually-correct and expensive: they let it happen two dozen times first. **Hashing the relevant state and comparing between iterations stops it on the second one.** And every halt needs a metric per reason, because a rising stuck count is a tool failing in a way the model cannot interpret, which is a bug report rather than a capacity problem.

d.title: Six stages in deploy order, and the recovery cost rises along it
d.caption: **The last row breaks the mental model the other five share.** Every stage above it recovers by returning to the previous artifact; a migration has already changed the database, and rolling back the application does not roll back the schema. **So stage 6 is the only one where the prevention is mandatory rather than advisable** — expand-and-contract is what keeps a code rollback available, and without it a failed deploy leaves old code against a new database with no fast way back.

d.title: A tag can be moved; a digest cannot
d.caption: **This is the mechanism behind a whole class of incident: the team performs the correct rollback, observes no improvement, and reasonably concludes the problem is elsewhere.** The release moved the tag, so redeploying that tag deploys the broken image again — an action that looks like a fix and is a no-op. Referencing the digest makes the rollback deterministic. **And the second failure in this chain is somebody else's retention policy:** the recovery path depends on an artifact that a registry default may have deleted.

d.title: Validating at import turns a bad config into a failed rollout
d.caption: **A value checked at first use means the deploy succeeded, the probe passed and the rollout completed before anything is wrong** — by which time the previous version may be gone. A process that refuses to start is never marked ready, so the orchestrator keeps the old pods and the bad configuration never takes traffic: the failure heals itself. **And `extra="forbid"` is the line that catches the characteristic configuration failure**, which is not a missing value but a mistyped name silently falling back to a default nobody chose.

d.title: The arithmetic that turns a successful autoscale into an outage
d.caption: **Each process has its own pool and knows nothing about the others, so the limit that matters is the product.** Four replicas at fifteen connections is comfortable against a hundred; scaling to eight is not, and the symptom is database errors with no code fault anywhere — affecting every service sharing that database, not only yours. **All three runtime bounds default to effectively unlimited**, which is why runtime failures are almost all one shape: a resource nobody capped.

state: OVER - a scale-up is an outage
